title: World Duty Free Company Limited v. Republic of Kenya
citation: ICSID Case No. ARB/00/7, Award Oct. 4, 2006, 46 I.L.M. 339 (2007)
lead: A duty-free operator sought relief for alleged state interference with its airport investment, but its own disclosure showed that a bribe had procured the agreement. The tribunal dismissed the contract-dependent claims on public-policy and avoidance grounds while retaining authority under the arbitration clause.

actors.name: World Duty Free Company Limited
actors.role: Isle of Man claimant substituted for House of Perfume

actors.name: Nasir Ibrahim Ali
actors.role: Signatory and project manager controlling the contracting companies

actors.name: Daniel arap Moi
actors.role: Former Kenyan president involved in the payment but not a party

proceedings: Arbitration commenced in June 2000. After the claimant disclosed the payment in December 2002, Kenya invoked illegality and expressly avoided in April 2003. Following a confined January 2006 hearing, the tribunal dismissed the claim on October 4, 2006, with each side bearing its legal costs and half the arbitration costs.
limits: The tribunal did not decide the alleged later breaches or damages, convict Moi, order restitution, or dismiss for lack of arbitral jurisdiction. No independent proprietary or restitutionary claim remained pleaded. The dispositive text said dismissed, without adding with prejudice.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The airport investment began with a concealed payment
sections.cue: Introduce the procurement events and precise money account.
paragraphs: Nasir Ibrahim Ali sought permissions for duty-free airport facilities through House of Perfume. Intermediary Rashid Sajjad arranged an audience with Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi and told Ali a $2 million personal cash donation was required to do business with the government. Ali transferred that amount through the intermediary. His account described $500,000 converted to Kenyan shillings in a briefcase brought to the president’s residence; afterward he found corn in place of the money. The record did not place the whole $2 million visibly in that single briefcase.

Ali said the payment appeared to be a bribe but that he was told it was lawful and necessary for the contract. He treated it as consideration paid for House of Perfume. These facts later came from his own written statement and hearing evidence.

sections.title: Related instruments established the operating rights
sections.cue: Explain the contracting company and governing law.
paragraphs: On April 27, 1989, Kenya agreed with House of Perfume to build, maintain, and operate duty-free complexes at Nairobi and Mombasa airports. The term was ten years with a further ten-year option on the same conditions except renegotiated rent, initially $1 million annually for both complexes. A May 11, 1990 amendment substituted World Duty Free Company Limited, an Isle of Man company. Ali signed for both companies and managed the project, retaining direct and indirect share interests after ownership changes.

The Kenya Airports Authority, for the government, signed a related lease August 25, 1995, running ten years from July 1, 1990 on the agreement’s terms. Article 9 authorized arbitration before the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes, or ICSID, for agreement or investment disputes and specified English law; Article 10(A) specified Kenyan law for construction. The tribunal later found no material conflict because Kenyan contract law incorporated English common law subject to local modifications and both sides accepted the relevant principles. It did not choose one system exclusively.

sections.title: The company alleged seizure and state interference
sections.cue: Present the competing accounts left undecided.
paragraphs: World Duty Free alleged spending about $27 million on facilities officially opened in 1990. It claimed political and private actors implicated it without consent in false Goldenberg gold-export documentation, seized control and assets through forged ownership claims and court receivers, frustrated legal remedies, and caused Ali’s unlawful arrest and deportation. It also alleged a duplicate company and diversion of the lease. It attributed the conduct to Kenya and sought restoration plus financial relief or roughly $500 million in alternative compensation, including lost profits and exemplary damages.

Kenya denied breach and loss, characterized the ownership conflict as private, contested attributing Pattni’s conduct to the state, raised limitations and unpaid rent, and disputed the deportation account. The tribunal would not resolve those competing allegations: all pleaded claims depended on the agreement, with no independent noncontractual proprietary or restitutionary claim remaining.

sections.title: The arbitration narrowed to procurement and enforceability
sections.cue: Trace the procedural stage that produced the award.
paragraphs: The claimant commenced ICSID proceedings in June 2000. Early disputes involved removal and restoration on the Isle of Man corporate register and whether directors or receivers controlled the case. An April 26, 2002 Manx order placed representation with directors and their appointed lawyers. Remaining preliminary objections were joined to the merits. The tribunal also distinguished public discussion from unauthorized disclosure of closed-hearing records.
Arbitrator James Crawford resigned in January 2001 after the claimant raised his connection to Kenya’s law firm; V. V. Veeder replaced him alongside President Gilbert Guillaume and Andrew Rogers.

After disclosure of the payment in the claimant’s December 2002 memorial, Kenya sought dismissal for illegality in March 2003 and expressly avoided the agreement in its April 18 counter-memorial. A January 18, 2006 preliminary merits hearing addressed only entitlement to avoid, loss of that right, and public policy. Breach and damages were excluded. Lord Mustill’s English-law opinion was Kenya’s legal submission, not expert proof of disputed facts.

sections.title: The tribunal found procurement bribery
sections.cue: Explain the finding and the transnational policy ground.
paragraphs: Kenya did not dispute the payment circumstances; the parties disputed characterization. World Duty Free invoked protocol gifts and Harambee, a tradition of collective contributions for public purposes. The tribunal rejected that explanation for concealed payments intended chiefly to obtain approval for this investment. It found bribery procuring the agreement, not merely purchasing an audience.

The tribunal distinguished narrow domestic policy for foreign-award recognition from objectively established transnational consensus. Criminal laws, international anticorruption instruments, national judgments, and arbitral precedents demonstrated condemnation of bribery. Some conventions postdated the transaction and bound only relevant parties from relevant dates; they confirmed condemnation rather than imposing retroactive treaty liability. Kenyan law already prohibited this conduct in 1989.

Comparative precedents distinguished unproved accusations from established corruption. Widespread corrupt practice did not make bribery acceptable. Contracts for corruption and contracts obtained through it could not support claims before this tribunal. Its discussion of Lagergren’s earlier jurisdictional refusal did not adopt that procedural disposition here.

sections.title: The chosen laws independently barred the pleaded claims
sections.cue: Explain severance and the claimant’s comparative-fault argument.
paragraphs: Under the English common law applied, illegality protected the public rather than rewarding a virtuous defendant. An illegal transaction might still have proprietary consequences where title could be shown independently, but no such separate claim was pleaded.

Ali was the driving force and alter ego of both successive companies, so substitution did not improve the claimant’s position. The bribe was intrinsic to securing the whole investment. Secrecy and omission from the writing did not make it collateral; severance would disregard how the agreement was obtained.

The claimant urged balancing the president’s solicitation and later alleged wrongdoing. The tribunal found no authority in the applicable English law for that discretion and considered the facts unfavorable even if it existed. Ali’s committed investment had not been held hostage when he paid; he remained free to decline investing and chose the bribe. The tribunal acknowledged the troubling spectacle of Kenya relying on its former president’s corruption and the apparent lack of recovery or prosecution against him. Its answer was that the public-policy bar protected citizens and would likewise bind a culpable Kenya as claimant. It did not thereby decide every alleged later state wrong.

sections.title: Kenya had timely avoided without informed affirmation
sections.cue: Keep state knowledge and the arbitration clause distinct.
paragraphs: Bribery of the other party’s agent made the contract voidable at the principal’s option, not necessarily void from inception. Positive avoidance was required and informed affirmation could defeat it. The tribunal found Kenya first learned of the bribe through the December 2002 disclosure and promptly, unequivocally avoided in April 2003. A prior breach by an otherwise innocent principal did not itself remove that option.

For this agency inquiry, Moi’s corrupt knowledge was not attributed to the state whose interests he violated; an elected president was not identical to Kenya itself. Continued dealings without knowledge established no affirmation, waiver, or estoppel. Possible consequences of avoidance were unpleaded and undecided, and returning the bribe was not required.

Neither side argued or proved that bribery specifically procured Article 9. The tribunal assumed the arbitration clause remained valid for this proceeding and award, rather than treating unenforceability of the main agreement as elimination of arbitral jurisdiction.

sections.title: The claim was dismissed without a damages or criminal judgment
sections.cue: State the award and jurisdictional limits.
paragraphs: All three arbitrators signed the October 4, 2006 award. Kenya had validly avoided, had not lost that right, and public policy under both transnational and chosen-law principles barred the pleaded claims. The dispositive text dismissed the claim. Each side bore its own legal costs and half of tribunal and ICSID costs; despite Kenya’s success, public policy made ordinary successful-party shifting inappropriate.

Moi was neither a party nor represented or heard as a witness, and the tribunal expressly lacked jurisdiction over him. The award imposed no criminal penalty, contractual damages, restitution, or recovery of the bribe. Kenya had requested dismissal with prejudice, but the actual dispositive wording did not add that phrase. No separate opinion was reproduced.
